en: The Vidyāsthānopama-sūtra:
1. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
2. There the Blessed One addressed the monks.
3. Whether, monks, Tathāgatas arise or whether they do not arise, the world undergoes dissolution and it undergoes evolution.
[Fragment from Or.15009/83v]:
... where the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove...
...good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end...
I shall teach you a Dharma discourse called "The Simile of the Branches of Knowledge"; listen to it.
4 /// What is this Dharma-discourse? It is [the discourse] concerning the arising or the passing away of the Tathāgatas... ///
Regarding this phrasing, cf. *Daśottarasūtra* E.a–c 4:
When the world is dissolving, for the most part sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara heaven.

There they exist as beings with form, mind-made, complete, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all major and minor limbs, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, feeding on joy, nourished by joy, self-luminous, moving through the air, long-lived, and remaining for a long duration of time.
6. As the world evolves, various crafts and occupations become known.
7. Such as, for example: mantras, recitations, medicinal herbs, magical arts, and medical treatment.
The divine eye, supernatural power, and the appropriate vision of knowledge.
They do not understand the path leading to the cessation of suffering;
wandering on a wrong path without being hindered, they act like the immortals, seeing no way out.
c: Read *unmārgeṇa*, a scribal error for *unmārgeṇa*.

9. But at whatever time the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones arise in the world, having directly known all those worldly crafts and occupations as well as that which is supramundane, the Tathāgatas teach that which is the most excellent among all branches of knowledge.
Namely: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Cf. Pelliot Sanskrit bleu 375rw: /// (ārya)satyaṃ ayaṃ duḥkha[s](amuday). ///
That which the Tathāgatas teach is the most excellent of all sciences;
yet some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas individually understand everything—
mantras, recitations, medicinal herbs, magical arts, and medical treatments.
The divine eye and supernormal power have arisen; the vision of knowledge has arisen.
But they do not understand the path that leads to the cessation of suffering;
failing to understand that path which leads to the cessation of suffering,
they wander like immortals upon a wrong path, never reaching their destination.
Those who do not see the way out.
e: cf. Pelliot Sanskrit bleu 375r2: /// ... they wander, not being overcome by the immortals ...; read:
"But when compassionate Perfectly Awakened Ones arise in the world, they proclaim the True Dharma, which dispels all suffering."

bc: cf. Pelliot Sanskrit bleu 375v1: /// ... who proclaim the Dharma ...; cf. also the following paragraph: Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the noble eightfold path leading to the security of Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the two verses in paragraphs 14 and 15, see the *Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna* [57]; for the actual text, see the *Thesaurus Literaturae Buddhicae* (TLB): https://www2.hf.uio.no/polyglotta/index.php?page=library&bid=2:
"Only rarely, at some time or other, do Tathāgatas appear in the world—teachers of humans and gods, possessed of vision, who have transcended all conflict. (1)
Those who proclaim the Dharma that dispels all suffering— the suffering itself, the origin of suffering, and the transcendence of suffering— [are the true teachers].
The noble eightfold path, secure and leading to Nirvana. //2//
While that Dharma, which dispels all suffering, was being taught,
they destroyed ignorance through wisdom and did not undergo rebirth again.
17. With joyful minds, those bhikṣus rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The *Vidyāsthānopama-sūtra* is completed.
May there be protection! Svāhā to Kutkāt-tuṃsa!
